    Start · Why it is called that

    The Name

    Borges's Library of Babel, the owner's own paper Hedging the Wheel, and what "research, not advice" means once you read the code.

    The library that contains everything — and tells you nothing#

    In 1941 Jorge Luis Borges published a short story that imagined the universe as a library: an endless run of hexagonal galleries holding every book that could possibly be written — every permutation of the alphabet, shelved without order. Somewhere in the stacks sits every true sentence: the catalog of the library itself, the history of the future, the correct explanation of everything. But nearly every volume is gibberish, the true ones are indistinguishable from the almost-true ones, and the librarians spend their lives wandering the galleries looking for the room that would let them tell the difference.

    The market prints its own Library of Babel every day. Every headline, filing, options sweep, chart pattern, congressional disclosure and anonymous rumour is on the shelves by sunrise, and somewhere in that pile is this morning's one true thesis — surrounded by ten thousand volumes of noise that read exactly like it.

    Bablytics is built to be the catalog room. A boardroom of fifteen readers, each holding a different theory of what makes a book true — flow, statistics, levels, gaps, discipline, value, convexity, house edge, news, cycles — argues over the day's stacks, signs its names to what it finds, and is audited on every signature that evening. The tagline is the whole job description: signal among the stacks.

    The mark is one gallery of the library: a hexagon whose book spines read as candlesticks. Stack the galleries edge to edge and they tessellate into honeycomb — the Library was always a hive — which is why the app's two themes are a morning hive (honey gold and maroon, the MORNING 🐝 setting) and an evening court (black and green, the original EVENING 🦉 terminal). The same honeycomb tile seeps through every background in both, and through this guide.

    Story and source: “La biblioteca de Babel”, first published in El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan (1941) and collected in Ficciones (1944).

    A short history of the name#

    Through feature round 4 the project was called Stonks — The Boardroom, and a few traces are deliberate. The repository folder is still ~/Stonks. The legacy STONKS_* environment variables (STONKS_MODEL, STONKS_MOCK, STONKS_HOST, STONKS_PORT) still work as fallbacks for the BABLYTICS_* spellings. An old data/stonks.db is renamed to data/bablytics.db automatically on first start. The board kept its cast and its furniture: the Boardroom, the Court of Owls and the Evening Court are unchanged, because Bablytics is the product and the board is its cast.

    If an old .env still says STONKS_MOCK=1, it is honoured exactly like BABLYTICS_MOCK=1. See Run from Source for the full variable list.

    Hedging the Wheel — the owner's paper#

    One seat at the table is built from a paper rather than from a person or a school. Hedging the Wheel is an adversarial-collaboration study, co-authored by this tool's owner with Claude, that exhaustively enumerated hedged, progressive and martingale betting systems against a fixed negative edge and asked which of them could change the outcome. Its results are the house rules the board argues under, and the Croupier 🎡 is the seat that brings them to every trade. In the code's own words the study found one survivor — the ratchet exit, attached to concentrated variance — and its steelman section is the part the Library tells you to read first: the system's real merits are variance control and pre-commitment, mislabeled as return.

    The theorems, as the Croupier's prompt states them:

    1. Expected P&L = edge × amount wagered, invariant to bet geometry. Spread, fees and theta are the vig. The first question for every candidate is where is the edge? — a live catalyst, informed flow, a demonstrable mispricing. If none is identifiable the expectation is minus-the-vig, and no sizing, hedging or structuring changes that.
    2. Diversification is a variance instrument; it cannot change a mean. Many expressions of the same macro bet narrow the outcome distribution around the same expectation while multiplying costs — that is covering the wheel, not diversifying. Name the cluster (crude complex, index short, crypto beta, defensive rotation) and penalise a candidate whose only appeal is being another copy of a bet the book already holds in better form.
    3. Bold play beats timid play (Dubins–Savage). Without positive edge, the probability of reaching a target is maximised by the fewest, largest, most concentrated bets followed by exit; spreading thin is provably inferior.
    4. The ratchet is real, but only on variance. A trailing-stop or profit-ratchet genuinely improves the odds of a winning session — attached to concentrated, high-variance positions. Attached to a hedged low-variance book it harvests nothing.
    5. Never martingale. Averaging down concentrates the largest wagers exactly where losses cluster.
    6. Frequent small wins are a reinforcement schedule, not evidence of edge. Be merciless with negative-skew structures that “usually work”.

    Those rules are not confined to one seat. Here is where the paper shows up in the code:

    The Croupier
    The seat itself — the house-edge analyst whose grade asks where is the edge and whose comment names the cluster a candidate belongs to and the ratchet that would make a high-variance bet coherent. Profile on The Board.
    The Executive's book-level rules
    The chair's prompt carries the paper's book-level rules: rank several top leads that are the same macro bet as one bet with the best expression on top; prefer fewer, better-edged ideas over coverage; state a pre-committed ratchet or exit for every high-variance idea in the top ranks; and end the memo with the day's HOUSE RULES — stakes discipline, exit rules and windfall policy, decided before the open, never mid-session. See Morning Briefing.
    The Glazier's fourth point
    The gap fade carries negative skew, so sizing and stops matter more than the base rate — “the house Hedging-the-Wheel rules apply, and a fade without a pre-committed stop is a donation schedule.”
    The Bailiff's 14:35 ratchet check
    A weekday job that evaluates the standing crude settle rail and reports BANK-HALF or no action. It executes nothing, because “bank half” is a sizing decision the record cannot infer. See The Bailiff.
    The Library
    The Croupier's shelf: the paper itself, Dubins & Savage's How to Gamble If You Must, Thorp's A Man for All Markets, Epstein's The Theory of Gambling and Statistical Logic. See News, Library & Archive.
    House rule.

    Markets are not roulette, but the theorems transfer wherever edge is absent: diversification cannot change a mean, costs are the vig, bold play beats timid spreading, and exits decided before play are the only defence that holds. That is why every morning memo closes with rules written before the bell, and why the board is graded on whether it honoured them.

    What “research, not advice” means in practice#

    Every page of the app and of this guide carries the same strip, and it is not decoration. The phrase is a description of what the code does and refuses to do. Concretely:

    • Nothing executes. The Pulse package has no order path — it imports no broker module and never touches the staged-order tables — and every payload is stamped “Model opinion — not financial advice; nothing executes.” The Bailiff acts on the record only: the board's own book and the Paper League, never a broker, and every surface says “The Bailiff closes legs in the record only — never the broker, never your money.” The Paper League is paper: fifteen $100,000 accounts that exist to score philosophies, not to move money.
    • The only real-money path is human-gated, one order at a time. If you connect Schwab, the bot stages up to five orders after each morning run. A staged order goes nowhere until you click submit on that one order, behind a confirmation that restates ticker, side, quantity and price. There is no “submit all”, no server-side loop over orders and no standing auto-submit setting; the client's order function is reached from exactly one place, per one explicit request. See Broker.
    • Grades are model output. Every grade is an integer 0–100 produced by a language model playing a persona — or, without an API key, by a deterministic heuristic in mock mode, which the UI labels. Four personas are inspired by the public philosophies of real people (Sam Parikh, Warren Buffett, Benjamin Graham, Nassim Taleb); they paraphrase published ideas for personal research and are not the people, not affiliated, not endorsed.
    • It is built for one person's own account posture. Bablytics is a local, single-user tool. It keeps its data in SQLite and plain files on your machine; the outbound traffic is market data, RSS feeds, the congressional-trade sources, the Anthropic API only when you add a key, and Schwab only if you connect it. See Data & Privacy.
    • Accountability runs both ways. The court grades the board every evening; the app also asks you to mark which leads you actually took and, once a taken trade has a realized outcome, to write a reflection — and when the trade lost, to say what you would do differently before the record accepts it. The Executive reads those reflections, verbatim, in the Evening Court. See Positions & Trades.

    The full statement — options risk, model output, no fiduciary relationship, the owner's-own-account posture — is on Not Financial Advice. Read it once; then read the board the way it reads the market: as a library that is mostly noise, with the occasional true volume that still has to be checked against the tape.
